question: What is the primary neurotransmitter blocked by anticholinergic drugs?
explanation: Anticholinergic drugs work by blocking the actions of acetylcholine at receptor sites. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T7#GNS223_U6_T7_h1)

question: Why does an anticholinergic drug need to cross the blood-brain barrier to help with brain disorders?

options.A: To speed up the breakdown of extra dopamine
options.B: To stop the drug from entering the bloodstream
options.C: To reach target receptors located inside the brain
options.D: To block heart receptors right away

explanation: Makes total sense! For a drug to treat a condition in the central nervous system, it has to be able to cross that protective blood-brain barrier to get where it's needed.

question: Which specific brain receptors do central anticholinergics block?
explanation: Central anticholinergics target and block muscarinic receptors to reduce cholinergic activity. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T7#GNS223_U6_T7_h2)

question: How do anticholinergic drugs help bring back balance in movement disorders?

options.A: By growing new nerves in the basal ganglia
options.B: By increasing dopamine production in the spinal cord
options.C: By blocking overactive acetylcholine to balance out low dopamine
options.D: By destroying extra acetylcholine enzymes in the liver

explanation: You're learning fast! In conditions like Parkinson's, when dopamine goes down, acetylcholine takes over too much. Blocking that excess acetylcholine restores smooth chemical balance.

question: Which of the following is a commonly used synthetic central anticholinergic drug?
explanation: Benztropine is a well-known synthetic anticholinergic used primarily for movement disorders. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T7#GNS223_U6_T7_h3)

question: Why can a common allergy pill like diphenhydramine cause anticholinergic effects in the brain?

options.A: It lowers blood pressure to slow down brain activity
options.B: It naturally has strong central anticholinergic properties
options.C: It turns into dopamine inside the liver
options.D: It permanently destroys peripheral acetylcholine receptors

explanation: Exactly! Many older allergy medications (antihistamines) easily cross into the brain and block muscarinic receptors, which is why they can make you drowsy or dry you out.

question: What is a primary indication for prescribing central anticholinergic drugs?
explanation: Central anticholinergics are frequently used to help control tremors and stiffness in Parkinson's disease. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T7#GNS223_U6_T7_h4)

question: A patient on a strong psychiatric medication suddenly gets severe muscle stiffness and spasms. What drug class will the doctor most likely order?
explanation: Brilliant! Anticholinergics are the go-to treatment for those pesky extrapyramidal side effects (muscle spasms and stiffness) caused by some antipsychotic drugs.

question: Which symptom is a classic peripheral adverse effect of anticholinergic drugs?
explanation: Blocking parasympathetic activity decreases saliva production, leading to noticeable dry mouth. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T7#GNS223_U6_T7_h5)

question: Why are elderly patients at much higher risk for brain-related side effects from anticholinergic drugs?

options.A: Their kidneys flush out the medication way too fast
options.B: Their bodies make way too much natural acetylcholine
options.C: They don't have any muscarinic receptors left in their body
options.D: Their blood-brain barrier is more sensitive and lets more drug through

explanation: You nailed it. Older adults are much more prone to confusion and fuzziness from these drugs because their brains and nervous systems handle these shifts more sensitively.

question: Which eye condition is an absolute contraindication for anticholinergic medications?
explanation: Anticholinergics dilate the pupil, which can trap fluid inside the eye and dangerously worsen glaucoma. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T7#GNS223_U6_T7_h6)

question: Why must men with an enlarged prostate be very careful with central anticholinergics?

options.A: Prostate tissue destroys the active drug instantly
options.B: The medication causes the prostate to shrink too fast
options.C: The drugs can cause or worsen trouble passing urine
options.D: Enlarged prostates absorb the drug too quickly into the blood

explanation: Spot on! By blocking acetylcholine, these drugs relax the bladder muscle and tighten the urinary outlet, making it really hard to pee if the prostate is already blocking things.

question: What important safety advice should a nurse give a patient about stopping anticholinergic drugs?

options.A: Stop taking them right away if your mouth feels dry
options.B: Reduce the dose slowly as advised by your doctor
options.C: Crush all the tablets so they clear your system faster
options.D: Double the dose if your tremors start coming back

explanation: You've got it! Stopping these meds suddenly can cause rebound muscle stiffness and make tremors flare up fiercely. Always taper safely!

question: What simple comfort measure can a nurse suggest for a patient dealing with dry mouth from these drugs?

options.A: Take small sips of water often or suck on sugarless sweets
options.B: Stop drinking all fluids for the rest of the day
options.C: Take your medication right before doing heavy exercise
options.D: Rinse your mouth with strong salt water every single hour

explanation: Brilliant nursing care! Frequent sips of water or sugarless candy keep those mucous membranes nice and comfortable without messing with their blood sugar.
